```{r setup}
library(hcttest)
```

## Study summaries

The earlier proof of Bulus (2026), Table 3, reanalyzes data from Zhang et al. (2023). The supplied
29-row dataset transcribes the displayed rounded group summaries. The first
group is sexual minority families; the second is heterosexual families. The
source image notes that the underlying data were reproduced under CC BY-NC.

```{r summaries}
studies <- readRDS(system.file("extdata", "table3-studies.rds", package = "hcttest"))
summary_table <- studies[, c("study", "n1", "m1", "sd1", "n2", "m2", "sd2")]
names(summary_table) <- c("Study - subgroup", "SM n", "SM mean", "SM SD",
                          "Heterosexual n", "Heterosexual mean", "Heterosexual SD")
print(summary_table, row.names = FALSE)
```

## Effect sizes and inverse-variance weights

The batch function returns yi (the standardized estimate) and vi (its squared
reported SE). It does not calculate normalized weights or percentages. Here we
calculate the weights directly as:

\[
  w_i = 1/v_i.
\]

These are unnormalized fixed-effect inverse-variance weights. Their sum is not
constrained; the batch function now also fits REML pooled models by default through metafor.
The constant and HC2 calculations use explicitly selected regression df,
central-t intervals, and the existing small-sample correction.

```{r calculate}
constant <- meta.robust.smd(studies, study = "study", method = "constant",
                            df = "regression", ss.adjust = TRUE, ci = "ct")
hc2 <- meta.robust.smd(studies, study = "study", method = "hc2",
                       df = "regression", ss.adjust = TRUE, ci = "ct")
results <- data.frame(
  study = studies$study,
  g = constant$yi,
  constant_lower = constant$lcl,
  constant_upper = constant$ucl,
  constant_weight = 1 / constant$vi,
  hc2_lower = hc2$lcl,
  hc2_upper = hc2$ucl,
  hc2_weight = 1 / hc2$vi)
print(results, row.names = FALSE)
```

Reported normalized weights from the source image remain in the dataset for
provenance but are not displayed or compared here. They cannot determine the
absolute unnormalized weights without the original normalization total. The
numbers above use our current formulas and selected settings; they are not a
claim of exact reproduction of the paper's reported analysis.

Several rows come from the same named study. This vignette computes separate
study/outcome effects and weights. Its default pooled fit assumes independent rows, without a covariance model.
Theoretical context is in the paper's Method section, Table 1, Appendix A2,
and Implications for Meta-Analysis. Weighted SMD SE approximations and the
current implementation still require their own validation.

## Reference

Bulus, M. (2026). Robust standard errors and confidence intervals for standardized
mean difference. *Research Synthesis Methods*. Advance online publication.

## Plotting study estimates

Both styles use the same default x-axis range. The ordinary plot uses the
stored effect-size intervals. The shaded plot uses 95% and 99% bands from the fitted central-t method
and its fitted degrees of freedom.
Study names are retained on the left.

```{r study-plots, fig.width=8, fig.height=9}
plot(hc2, margins = c(-0.2, 0.2), main = "HC2 study estimates")
plot(hc2, pretty = TRUE, margins = c(-0.2, 0.2),
     main = "HC2 study estimates", label.padding = 1)
```

The two variance methods can also be displayed together. Rows match by study
name; colors identify the methods. Both plots preserve the fitted central-t
interval method. The two estimates appear above and below each study label.

```{r compare-study-plots, fig.width=8, fig.height=9}
plot(constant, hc2, pretty = TRUE, col = c("navy", "darkorange3"),
     margins = c(-0.2, 0.2), main = "Constant and HC2 estimates")
legend("bottomright", legend = c("Constant", "HC2"),
       col = c("navy", "darkorange3"), lwd = 3, bty = "n")
```

## Pooled estimates

The pooled attribute reports raw and standardized summaries. The model choice
can affect both heterogeneity and the pooled point estimate. Lines in each
model color mark its pooled effect in the study plots.

```{r pooled-estimates}
print(attr(constant, "pooled"), row.names = FALSE)
print(attr(hc2, "pooled"), row.names = FALSE)
```

## Multiple outcomes within one study

Analyze and display each outcome separately. No pooled effect is calculated
across outcomes measured on the same people.

```{r multiple-outcomes, fig.width=8, fig.height=6}
dat <- subset(iris, Species != "virginica")
outcomes <- c("Sepal.Length", "Sepal.Width", "Petal.Length", "Petal.Width")
constant.multi <- multi.robust.smd(dat, outcomes, "Species", method = "constant",
                                  ci = "ct")
hc2.multi <- multi.robust.smd(dat, outcomes, "Species", method = "hc2", ci = "ct")
print(constant.multi[, c("outcome", "yi", "se", "lcl.equivalence", "ucl.equivalence")],
      row.names = FALSE)
print(hc2.multi[, c("outcome", "yi", "se", "lcl.equivalence", "ucl.equivalence")],
      row.names = FALSE)
plot(constant.multi, hc2.multi, pretty = TRUE,
     col = c("#001F3F", "#B35400"))
```

SMD equivalence intervals and bound tests inherit `ci = "z"`, `"ct"`, or
`"nct"`. At `alpha = 0.05`, individual outcome rows show 90% equivalence
intervals, with ribbon fading to 95%. Raw-difference equivalence uses central-t
inference. The default reference is zero. Meta-analysis plots continue to show
their fitted metafor pooled summaries below the tick labels.
